claim: amotl2a is expressed in the pLLP throughout migration with reduced or no expression in the most leading and trailing domains.
source: By combining in situ hybridization (ISH) with Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) immunostaining in cldnb:gfp transgenic embryos, we showed that amotl2a was expressed throughout migration (Figure 1A–C) in most of the pLLP with reduced or no expression in the most leading and trailing domains (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental ISH and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-I.

claim: amot, amotl1, and amotl2b are not expressed in the pLLP.
source: The other motin genes amot, amotl1, and amotl2b were not expressed in the pLLP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Amotl2a-TdT is present in the cytoplasm and strongly concentrated at the most apical, constricted part of cells in assembling proneuromasts.
source: Amotl2a-TdT was present in the cytoplasm and was strongly concentrated at the most apical, constricted part of the cells in assembling proneuromasts (Figure 1J–K′).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing Amotl2a-TdT localization in Figure 1J-K'.

claim: Amotl2a-TdT appears as an apical ring in deposited neuromasts.
source: In addition, it appeared as an apical ring in deposited neuromasts (Figure 1L,L′).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 1L,L'.

claim: FGF signaling is necessary for amotl2a expression in the pLLP.
source: amotl2a expression was specifically lost in the pLLP of fgf3−/−;fgf10−/− double mutants (Figure 1M–R), upon expression of a dominant negative FGFR1 receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–I), and in embryos treated with the FGFR inhibitor SU5402 (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by loss-of-function experiments in FGF mutants and pharmacological inhibition shown in Figure 1M-R and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-I.

claim: FGF signaling is sufficient for amotl2a expression in the pLLP.
source: Conversely, ectopic activation of FGF signaling using the Tg(hsp70l:fgf3-Myc)zf115 transgenic line led to an expansion of the amotl2a expression domain in the pLLP as compared to controls (Figure 1S–X and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by gain-of-function experiments using FGF overexpression shown in Figure 1S-X and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J,K.

claim: Amotl2aMo efficiently blocks the translation of a fusion between the ATG region of amotl2a and GFP.
source: At low doses, Amotl2aMo did not lead to any obvious morphological defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D) (Wang et al., 2011) and efficiently blocked the translation of a fusion between the ATG region of amotl2a and GFP (MoBS_Amotl2a-GFP, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by morpholino validation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F and cited from Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Amotl2a is not essential for tight junction assembly in the pLLP.
source: While mature rosettes had similarly strong apical actin and ZO1 staining in morphant and control embryos (white arrows in Figure 2C–F), the distance between the tip of the pLLP and the most recent fully assembled rosette (yellow arrows), appeared increased in amotl2a morphants (double arrowhead in Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ZO1 and phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 2A-F.

claim: Rosette assembly is slightly delayed in amotl2a morphants.
source: While mature rosettes had similarly strong apical actin and ZO1 staining in morphant and control embryos (white arrows in Figure 2C–F), the distance between the tip of the pLLP and the most recent fully assembled rosette (yellow arrows), appeared increased in amotl2a morphants (double arrowhead in Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing increased distance to assembled rosettes in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Neuromasts are deposited normally in amotl2a morphants.
source: Yet, neuromasts were deposited normally (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2G,H.

claim: The pLLP of amotl2a morphant embryos migrates 35% slower than controls.
source: In addition, the pLLP of amotl2a morphant embryos migrated 35% slower than controls (Figure 2I–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging and migration speed quantification shown in Figure 2I-M.

claim: All amotl2a morphant primordia reach the tip of the tail.
source: Yet, all primordia reached the tip of the tail (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Expression of cxcr4b and cxcr7b is not detectably affected in amotl2a morphants.
source: Expression of the two G-protein-coupled receptors cxcr4b and cxcr7b was not detectably affected in morphants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that a deregulation of their expression is unlikely to account for the decrease in migration speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The size of amotl2a morphant pLLP is increased throughout the migration process.
source: Interestingly, the size of amotl2a morphant pLLP appeared obviously increased throughout the migration process (Figure 3A–C, also Figure 2I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 3A-C and Figure 2I,J.

claim: The number of cells in amotl2a morphant pLLP is increased by 35–38% as compared to either uninjected or p53Mo-injected embryos.
source: Cell counts indicated that the number of cells in amotl2a morphant pLLP was increased by 35–38% as compared to either uninjected or p53Mo-injected embryos (Figure 3E, p = 1.58E-40 and p = 9.53E-31, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by automated cell counting data shown in Figure 3E with statistical significance.

claim: Co-injection of Amotl2aMo with amotl2am RNA partially rescues the morphant phenotype.
source: Co-injection of Amotl2aMo with amotl2am RNA partially rescued the morphant phenotype (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: Overexpression of amotl2a at high concentration induces a moderate but significant decrease in cell number (-15%, p = 5.20E-07).
source: While overexpression of amotl2a at the concentration used for the rescue experiment did not significantly reduce the number of cells in the pLLP (Figure 3F), injection at a higher concentration induced a moderate, but significant decrease in cell number (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, −15%, p = 5.20E-07).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data from overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a significant increase in the EdU index of about 15% in the pLLP of amotl2a morphants as compared to controls.
source: There was a significant increase in the EdU index of about 15% in the pLLP of amotl2a morphants as compared to controls (Figure 3J, p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: There is a 34% increase in proliferation in the trailing region of amotl2a morphant pLLP compared to controls.
source: While there was no difference in the proliferation index in the leading region between morphants and controls, there was a 34% increase in the trailing region (Figure 3K, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU proliferation assay data analyzed separately for leading and trailing regions shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Two TALEN-induced amotl2a alleles (fu45 and fu46) introduce a frame-shift and a premature STOP codon in the third exon.
source: Among several identified amotl2a alleles, two were further analyzed that introduced a frame-shift and a premature STOP codon in the third exon (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data and schematic representation in Figure 4A.

claim: Both amotl2a mutant alleles (fu45 and fu46) have identical phenotypes.
source: Both alleles had identical phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is stated based on phenotypic analysis of the two alleles.

claim: amotl2a−/− homozygous mutants are morphologically indistinguishable from their siblings.
source: amotl2a−/− homozygous mutants were morphologically indistinguishable from their siblings (Figure 4C–F) but had larger primordia (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 4C-F.

claim: amotl2a−/− mutants have larger primordia than siblings.
source: amotl2a−/− homozygous mutants were morphologically indistinguishable from their siblings (Figure 4C–F) but had larger primordia (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Cell number in amotl2a−/− mutant pLLP is increased by 21% compared to siblings.
source: Cell count analyses revealed a significant increase in cell numbers of 21% in amotl2a−/− mutants as compared to their siblings (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: pLLP migrates 32% slower in amotl2a−/− mutants compared to controls (p < 0.0001).
source: In addition and as in morphants, pLLP migrated slower in amotl2a−/− mutants as compared to controls (−32%, p < 0.0001, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by migration speed quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell counts in MZamotl2a−/− mutant pLLP are increased by 40% compared to controls (p = 1.18E-21).
source: pLLP cell counts were further increased to 40% in MZamotl2a−/− mutants as compared to controls (Figure 4J–L, p = 1.18E-21), an increase similar to that quantified in amotl2a morphants (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data in Figure 4J-L with statistical significance.

claim: Deposited neuromasts and interneuromast chains do not contain more cells at 48 hpf in amotl2a morphants compared to controls.
source: Neither deposited neuromasts nor interneuromast chains comprised more cells at 48 hpf in morphants as compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data in deposited structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MZamotl2a−/− mutant neuromasts contain the same number of cells as controls at 72 hpf.
source: Similarly, MZamotl2a−/− mutant neuromasts also contained the same number of cells as controls at 72 hpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data in neuromasts shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There is on average one additional neuromast deposited in amotl2a morphants and mutants compared to control embryos.
source: Yet, there was on average one additional neuromast deposited in morphants (not shown) and mutants (Figure 4M–O) as compared to control embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuromast counting data shown in Figure 4M-O.

claim: Yap1 and Taz were identified as potential Amotl2a interaction-partners in a Y2H screen with scores A and B, respectively.
source: 25 proteins were identified as potential Amotl2a interaction-partners and were given a score ranging from A (very high confidence in the interaction) to D (moderate confidence in the interaction). The Hippo pathway effectors Yap1 and Taz were among the 10 strongest identified partners with an A and B score, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H screen results.

claim: The Selected Interaction Domain of Yap1 and Taz includes the evolutionarily conserved WW motifs (2 for Yap1 and 1 for Taz).
source: Further analysis showed that in both cases, the amino acid (aa) sequence shared by all prey fragments (Selected Interaction Domain) included the evolutionarily conserved WW motifs (2 for Yap1 and 1 for Taz, Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H screen analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations of the WW motifs of Yap1 and Taz abolish the interaction with Amotl2a.
source: Furthermore, mutations of the WW motifs of Yap1 and Taz abolished the corresponding interaction with Amotl2a (pink in Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutations of the LPTY and PPEY motifs of Amotl2a abolish the interaction with WT Yap1 and Taz.
source: Conversely, mutations of the LPTY and PPEY motifs of Amotl2a, but not of either of them alone, abolished the interaction with WT Yap1 and Taz (green and yellow, respectively, in Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Zebrafish yap1 and taz are broadly expressed during development including in the pLLP.
source: Both genes were broadly expressed during development including in the pLLP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The pLLP of yap1 morphant embryos has about 15% less cells than uninjected controls (p = 2.65E-12).
source: Cell counts indicated that the pLLP of yap1 morphant embryos had about 15% less cells than uninjected controls (p = 2.65E-12) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 5E with statistical significance.

claim: yap1−/− pLLP shows a decrease in cell number of 19% (p = 1.25E-05).
source: Cell counts confirmed that yap1−/− pLLP also showed a decrease in cell number of 19% (p = 1.25E-05) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C with statistical significance.

claim: At 24 hpf, the pLLP of MZyap1−/− mutants is 15% smaller than related controls (p = 4.12E-08).
source: At 24 hpf, the pLLP of MZyap1−/− mutants was already 15% smaller than related controls (p = 4.12E-08).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data at 24 hpf with statistical significance.

claim: At 30 hpf, the pLLP of MZyap1−/− mutants is 21% smaller than related controls (p = 2.15E-10).
source: This difference continued to increase with time to reach 21% at 30 hpf (p = 2.15E-10) and 27% at 36 hpf (p = 2.41E-14) (Figure 5N–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data at 30 hpf shown in Figure 5N-P with statistical significance.

claim: At 36 hpf, the pLLP of MZyap1−/− mutants is 27% smaller than related controls (p = 2.41E-14).
source: This difference continued to increase with time to reach 21% at 30 hpf (p = 2.15E-10) and 27% at 36 hpf (p = 2.41E-14) (Figure 5N–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data at 36 hpf shown in Figure 5N-P with statistical significance.

claim: MZyap1−/− mutants do not show a decreased number of neuromasts.
source: Intriguingly, neither our morphants (not shown) nor our MZyap1−/− mutants showed a decreased number of neuromasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuromast counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MZyap1−/− mutant neuromasts do not contain fewer cells.
source: Furthermore, these neuromasts did not contain fewer cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data in neuromasts shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The number of hair cells per neuromast is not affected in MZyap1−/− mutants.
source: Intriguingly, neither the number of hair cells per neuromast (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H) nor the expression of prox1 in the pLLP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L′) was affected in our MZyap1−/− mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by hair cell counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: The expression of prox1 in the pLLP is not affected in MZyap1−/− mutants.
source: Intriguingly, neither the number of hair cells per neuromast (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H) nor the expression of prox1 in the pLLP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–L′) was affected in our MZyap1−/− mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data for prox1 shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I-L'.

claim: The number of cells in the pLLP of amotl2a;yap1 double morphants is significantly reduced by 34% as compared to amotl2a morphants (p = 1.53E-16).
source: Automated cell counts revealed that the number of cells in the pLLP of amotl2a;yap1 double morphants was significantly reduced as compared to amotl2a morphants (34% reduction, p = 1.53E-16) and was not significantly different from controls (p = 0.098) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by automated cell counting data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance.

claim: The number of cells in the pLLP of amotl2a;yap1 double morphants is not significantly different from controls (p = 0.098).
source: Automated cell counts revealed that the number of cells in the pLLP of amotl2a;yap1 double morphants was significantly reduced as compared to amotl2a morphants (34% reduction, p = 1.53E-16) and was not significantly different from controls (p = 0.098) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by automated cell counting data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance.

claim: The 37% increase in MZamotl2a−/− pLLP (p = 4.62E-11) is suppressed in MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− double mutants and comparable to controls (p = 0.06).
source: These observations were confirmed by automated cell counts: the 37% increase in MZamotl2a−/− pLLP (p = 4.62E-11) was suppressed in MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− double mutants and comparable to controls (p = 0.06).
evidence: The claim is supported by automated cell counting data with statistical significance.

claim: MZyap1−/− mutants have 27% fewer cells than MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− double mutants (p = 1.09E-11).
source: MZyap1−/− mutants were, however, still lower than double mutants (−27%, p = 1.09E-11) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E with statistical significance.

claim: The increased proliferation rate in the trailing region of amotl2a morphants is partially suppressed in embryos co-injected with Amotl2aMo and Yap1Mo (p = 0.003).
source: As previously observed, the proliferation rate in amotl2a morphants was significantly increased in the trailing region as compared to controls (control vs Amotl2aMo: 0.27 ± 0.01 and 0.40 ± 0.01, p < 0.0001); and this increase was partially suppressed in embryos co-injected with Amotl2aMo and Yap1Mo (0.32 ± 0.02, p = 0.003) (Figure 6F–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6F-K with statistical significance.

claim: amotl2am can partially rescue the increase in cell counts of amotl2a morphants (p = 6.36E-08).
source: While amotl2am could partially rescue the increase in cell counts of amotl2a morphants as shown above (p = 6.36E-08), amotl2amLP could not (p = 0.18) (Figure 6L–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6L-P with statistical significance.

claim: amotl2amLP cannot rescue the increase in cell counts of amotl2a morphants (p = 0.18).
source: While amotl2am could partially rescue the increase in cell counts of amotl2a morphants as shown above (p = 6.36E-08), amotl2amLP could not (p = 0.18) (Figure 6L–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6L-P with statistical significance.

claim: Wild-type Amotl2a and Amotl2a mutated in LPTY and PPEY motifs have comparable stability in yeast.
source: The two proteins had a comparable stability in yeast (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both amotl2a morphants and mutant embryos show a slight but significant expansion of the lef1 expression domain into the trailing region of the primordium as compared to their respective controls.
source: Both amotl2a morphants and mutant embryos showed a slight but significant expansion of the lef1 expression domain into the trailing region of the primordium as compared to their respective controls (Figure 7A–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data for lef1 shown in Figure 7A-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F-J.

claim: The expression of lef1 is not modified in MZyap1−/− mutants.
source: On the other hand, the expression of lef1 was not modified in MZyap1−/− mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1K–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by ISH data for lef1 shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1K-N.

claim: Cell counts in Lef1Mo-injected MZamotl2a−/− mutants are significantly reduced by 23% as compared to MZamotl2a−/− mutants (p = 5.32E-08).
source: While MZamotl2a−/− mutants showed bigger primordia as expected (36%, p = 2.89E-09) (Figure 7G, see 'a' in N), lef1 morphants at this stage did not show a significant reduction in pLLP cell counts (p = 0.1) (Figure 7F,J and 'b' in N). In contrast, cell counts in Lef1Mo-injected MZamotl2a−/− mutants were significantly reduced as compared to MZamotl2a−/− mutants (−23%, p = 5.32E-08, Figure 7N 'c') and equivalent to controls (p = 0.28, Figure 7N 'd').
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7N with statistical significance.

claim: Cell counts in Lef1Mo-injected MZamotl2a−/− mutants are equivalent to controls (p = 0.28).
source: In contrast, cell counts in Lef1Mo-injected MZamotl2a−/− mutants were significantly reduced as compared to MZamotl2a−/− mutants (−23%, p = 5.32E-08, Figure 7N 'c') and equivalent to controls (p = 0.28, Figure 7N 'd').
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7N with statistical significance.

claim: When MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− is injected with Lef1Mo, the number of cells in the pLLP is significantly lower by 19% than in MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− double mutants (p = 0.001).
source: Indeed when we injected MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− with Lef1Mo, the number of cells in the pLLP was significantly lower than in MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− double mutants (−19%, p = 0.001, Figure 7N 'f') and was not significantly different from that of MZyap1−/− mutants ('g' in Figure 7N, p = 0.07).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7N with statistical significance.

claim: When MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− is injected with Lef1Mo, the number of cells in the pLLP is not significantly different from that of MZyap1−/− mutants (p = 0.07).
source: Indeed when we injected MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− with Lef1Mo, the number of cells in the pLLP was significantly lower than in MZamotl2a−/−;MZyap1−/− double mutants (−19%, p = 0.001, Figure 7N 'f') and was not significantly different from that of MZyap1−/− mutants ('g' in Figure 7N, p = 0.07).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 7N with statistical significance.

claim: The Hippo signaling pathway plays a major role in organ growth control.
source: While the Hippo signaling pathway plays a major role in organ growth control, how it senses and responds to increased cell density is still unclear.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: The Hippo signaling pathway was first identified in Drosophila.
source: First identified in Drosophila (Pan, 2007), the Hippo signaling pathway is highly conserved in vertebrates (Halder and Johnson, 2010; Pan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pan, 2007.

claim: The Hippo signaling pathway is highly conserved in vertebrates.
source: First identified in Drosophila (Pan, 2007), the Hippo signaling pathway is highly conserved in vertebrates (Halder and Johnson, 2010; Pan, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Halder and Johnson, 2010 and Pan, 2010.

claim: Contact inhibition of proliferation is largely mediated by the Hippo signaling pathway.
source: Contact inhibition of proliferation was found to be largely mediated by the Hippo signaling pathway (Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: AMOT, AMOTL1, and AMOTL2 are scaffold proteins associated with tight-junctions, required for tight junction integrity.
source: AMOT, AMOTL1, and AMOTL2 are scaffold proteins associated with tight-junctions, required for tight junction integrity (Bratt et al., 2002; Sugihara-Mizuno et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2009) and endothelial cell migration (Troyanovsky et al., 2001; Bratt et al., 2005; Aase et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011; Hultin et al., 2014; Moleirinho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bratt et al., 2002; Sugihara-Mizuno et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2009.

claim: Motin proteins are required for endothelial cell migration.
source: AMOT, AMOTL1, and AMOTL2 are scaffold proteins associated with tight-junctions, required for tight junction integrity (Bratt et al., 2002; Sugihara-Mizuno et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2009) and endothelial cell migration (Troyanovsky et al., 2001; Bratt et al., 2005; Aase et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011; Hultin et al., 2014; Moleirinho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Troyanovsky et al., 2001; Bratt et al., 2005; Aase et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011; Hultin et al., 2014; Moleirinho et al., 2014.

claim: Motin proteins interact with YAP and TAZ via their PPxY motifs and the WW motifs of YAP and TAZ.
source: Recently, Motin proteins have further been shown to interact with YAP and TAZ via their PPxY motifs and the WW motifs of YAP and TAZ (Chan et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011; Hirate et al., 2013; Hong, 2013; Lucci et al., 2013; Yi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011; Hirate et al., 2013; Hong, 2013; Lucci et al., 2013; Yi et al., 2013.

claim: The physical interaction between Motin proteins and YAP/TAZ leads to the inhibition of YAP/TAZ via cytoplasmic retention, independent of the canonical Hippo pathway.
source: In most cases, this physical interaction leads to the inhibition of YAP/TAZ via cytoplasmic retention, similar to, but independent of the canonical Hippo pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature about Motin-YAP/TAZ interactions.

claim: There is a competition between YAP/TAZ and F-actin to bind to Motin proteins.
source: Interestingly, there is a competition between YAP/TAZ and F-actin to bind to Motin proteins (Mana-Capelli et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mana-Capelli et al., 2014.

claim: The pLL primordium consists of about 100 progenitors that delaminate from a cranial placode and migrate posteriorly towards the tip of the tail.
source: The pLL primordium (pLLP) consists of about 100 progenitors that delaminate from a cranial placode and migrate posteriorly towards the tip of the tail (Metcalfe et al., 1985; Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudiere, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Metcalfe et al., 1985; Ghysen and Dambly-Chaudiere, 2004.

claim: Proneuromast assembly requires Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF) signaling and the downstream effectors Shroom3 and Rock2a to activate non-muscle myosin and apical-constriction.
source: This assembly requires Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF) signaling and the downstream effectors Shroom3 and Rock2a to activate non-muscle myosin and apical-constriction (Lecaudey et al., 2008; Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008; Ernst et al., 2012; Harding and Nechiporuk, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lecaudey et al., 2008; Nechiporuk and Raible, 2008; Ernst et al., 2012; Harding and Nechiporuk, 2012.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling promotes proliferation in the leading region of the pLLP.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling partially compensates for this loss by promoting proliferation in the leading region (Gamba et al., 2010; Aman et al., 2011; McGraw et al., 2011; Valdivia et al., 2011; Matsuda et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gamba et al., 2010; Aman et al., 2011; McGraw et al., 2011; Valdivia et al., 2011; Matsuda et al., 2013.

claim: Amotl2a has been reported to be expressed in the migrating pLLP.
source: We focus on the role of the Motin protein Angiomotin-like 2a (Amotl2a) that has been reported to be expressed in the migrating pLLP, to be a target of FGF signaling (Huang et al., 2007), to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling during early zebrafish development (Li et al., 2012), and is a potential candidate to interact with the Hippo signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2007.

claim: Amotl2a is a target of FGF signaling.
source: We focus on the role of the Motin protein Angiomotin-like 2a (Amotl2a) that has been reported to be expressed in the migrating pLLP, to be a target of FGF signaling (Huang et al., 2007), to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling during early zebrafish development (Li et al., 2012), and is a potential candidate to interact with the Hippo signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2007.

claim: Amotl2a inhibits Wnt/β-catenin signaling during early zebrafish development.
source: We focus on the role of the Motin protein Angiomotin-like 2a (Amotl2a) that has been reported to be expressed in the migrating pLLP, to be a target of FGF signaling (Huang et al., 2007), to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling during early zebrafish development (Li et al., 2012), and is a potential candidate to interact with the Hippo signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Amotl2a limits proliferation in the trailing part of the pLLP by forming a ternary complex with Yap1 and β-catenin.
source: This leads us to propose that Amotl2a, possibly by forming a ternary complex with Yap1 and β-catenin, limits proliferation in the trailing part of the pLLP.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: This is the first report of a mechanism that limits proliferation in the pLLP.
source: Here, we report the first mechanism that limits proliferation in the pLLP.
evidence: The claim is stated by the authors based on their findings.

claim: This is the first report implicating the Hippo effector Yap1 in size control in the pLLP.
source: In addition, we implicate the Hippo effector Yap1 in size control in the pLLP for the first time.
evidence: The claim is stated by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Motin proteins play a major role in limiting organ growth during development by negatively regulating Yap/Taz and Wnt/β-catenin activities in vivo.
source: Altogether, our results strongly suggest that Motin proteins play a major role in limiting organ growth during development by negatively regulating Yap/Taz and Wnt/β-catenin activities in vivo.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The physical interaction between Amotl2a and Yap1 is required for the proliferation-limiting activity of Amotl2a.
source: Altogether, these results suggested that the physical interaction between Amotl2a and Yap1 is required for the proliferation-limiting activity of Amotl2a.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from rescue experiments with mutated Amotl2a.

claim: Amotl2a could link actomyosin-based cell shape changes such as columnarization and/or apical constriction during rosette assembly to Yap1 activity and proliferation.
source: It is thus tempting to propose that Amotl2a could link actomyosin-based cell shape changes such as columnarization and/or apical constriction during rosette assembly to Yap1 activity and proliferation.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the authors' data and known properties of Motin proteins.

claim: Loss of Amotl2a leads to uncoupling of proliferation from rosette assembly, resulting in hyperplastic pLLP and additional sensory organs.
source: Such a mechanism would allow to couple proliferation rate to organogenesis. Upon loss of Amotl2a, in contrast, this coupling would be lost so that proneuromasts assemble but proliferation is not restricted, leading to hyperplastic LLP and additional sensory organs.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic interpretation of the observed phenotypes.
